topics.label: Introduction and lecture framing
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture as an integration of previously introduced immune cells and molecules.

topics.label: Principles of innate danger recognition
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics establish how innate receptors distinguish microbial or damage signals through their specificity, inherited encoding and cellular location.

topics.label: Toll-like receptor recognition and signalling
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how toll-like receptors translate microbial recognition into immune responses appropriate to the location of the signal.

topics.label: Non-TLR danger sensing and inflammatory disease
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how sensing pathways beyond toll-like receptors activate inflammation that can contribute to disease.

topics.label: Sentinel-driven inflammation and leukocyte recruitment
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how activated sentinel cells generate inflammatory signals that mobilise leukocytes into infected tissue.

topics.label: Lymphatic drainage and adaptive immune priming
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how dendritic cells carry evidence of tissue infection through lymphatic drainage to initiate adaptive responses in lymph nodes.

topics.label: Excessive systemic inflammation and septic shock
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic examines how excessive inflammatory activation becomes a life-threatening systemic response.

topics.label: Passive and active resolution of inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how inflammation subsides through the loss of activating stimuli and the increasing influence of inhibitory signals.

topics.label: Tissue repair and persistent inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine why inflamed tissue may recover or remain chronically inflamed, with granulomas illustrating containment when infection cannot be cleared.

topics.label: Lecture close and next lecture
topics.groupedBecause: This closing ends the lecture and announces complement as the next lecture's subject.
